title: On Clusters and Constellations
caption: The globular cluster ESO 520-21, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Somewhere in this glittering field of stars is ESO 520-21, a globular cluster that also goes by Palomar 6, photographed with two of Hubble's cameras. A globular cluster is a densely packed, roughly spherical collection of stars.

ESO 520-21 sits near our galaxy's centre, where gas and dust between the stars absorb starlight and make observing harder. That absorption affects some wavelengths more than others, so objects look redder than they really are. Astronomers call this reddening, and it makes it particularly hard to work out the properties of clusters near the galactic centre.

The cluster sits in Ophiuchus, near the celestial equator. Ptolemy, an Egyptian astronomer of the second century, listed Ophiuchus among his 48 constellations, and all 48 still feature in the International Astronomical Union's official list of 88. Not every constellation survived history, though. Forgotten ones include Felis the Cat and Rangifer the Reindeer.

understand.summary: The image combines visible data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with near-infrared data from Wide Field Camera 3. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye and passes through dust more easily, helping reveal a cluster hidden behind the galactic centre's dust.
